column5: misuse of YHWH's name
column6: The command forbids bearing YHWH's name falsely and says the guilty will not be acquitted; it gives a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's secondary hearing of glorifying the name as keeping the Lord's identifying mark free from fault.

column5: blasphemy of the Name
column6: The narrative identifies a man who blasphemes and curses the Name; this directly intersects the commentary's concern for the Lord's name and its account of a denier whose contemptuous speech earns a bodily stigma.

column5: penalty for blaspheming the Name
column6: The same law sentences the blasphemer of YHWH's name to death; it adds a concrete sanction for dishonoring the name beside the commentary's punitive mark for dismissing revelation.

column5: sanctifying a profaned name
column6: YHWH says he will sanctify his great name, which Israel profaned among the nations; this directly develops the commentary's secondary sense of keeping the Lord's name-mark free of blemish, and makes public reputation part of the issue.

column5: nose and ears cut; survivors consumed by fire
column6: In the allegory of Jerusalem and Samaria's infidelity, enemies mutilate the women's faces and the remnant is consumed by fire; it supplies a concrete judgment-image of facial stigma joined to fire, while the context and instrument differ from the commentary's brand.

column5: Abel's blood cries from the ground
column6: Cain's hidden murder is disclosed when Abel's blood cries to God from the ground; this is a specific trace left on earth that reveals an act and its agent, enriching the commentary's claim that an effect can remain visible or unseen.

column5: Zion engraved on God's palms
column6: YHWH says Zion is engraved on his palms and continually before him; this reverses the commentary's owner-mark image, showing the marked person preserved in the owner's memory, and adds permanence to the trace.

column5: forehead plate and acceptance of offerings
column6: Aaron bears the guilt attached to the sacred gifts on the forehead plate so the offerings may be accepted; this continuation gives the inscribed holiness a cleansing and acceptance function beside the commentary's call to keep the Lord's mark pure.

column5: no hiding place from YHWH
column6: YHWH asks whether anyone can hide where he cannot see and says he fills heaven and earth; it directly specifies that concealed conduct remains within divine sight, as in the commentary's public/hidden pair.

column5: God reveals hidden things and knows darkness
column6: Daniel's prayer says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness; this supplies a close biblical-Aramaic formulation of divine knowledge of the concealed alongside the commentary's explicit open/hidden clause.

column5: book of remembrance for those who esteem YHWH's name
column6: A book of remembrance is written for those who fear YHWH and esteem his name; it makes devotion leave a durable written trace and connects remembrance of the name with later recognition.

column5: distinction between the righteous and the wicked
column6: The audience will again see a distinction between the righteous and wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not; this specifies the commentary's claim that a mark distinguishes one person from another by the allegiance it records.

column5: book of the covenant read aloud
column6: Moses reads the book of the covenant to Israel, who answer to its words; this gives a concrete scriptural witness for the commentary's contrast between dismissing ancient accounts as tales and receiving the earliest writings as revelation.

column5: Moses' scroll kept as a witness
column6: Moses orders the written law to be placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel; this directly illuminates the surah's appeal to the scrolls of Moses after the commentary's denier labels the stories of the ancients fables.

column5: Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt
column6: During the escape from Sodom, Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt; this is an individual bodily remnant within the same destruction story, later read in Wisdom 10:7 as a memorial, adding a concrete trace beside the commentary's ruined-city signs.

column5: secret speech is not hidden
column6: Wisdom says every utterance is heard and no secret whisper escapes; this gives a Jewish formulation of concealed speech remaining knowable, particularly apt beside the commentary's open/hidden knowledge and its judged denier's words.

column5: people inscribed and sealed for life or death
column6: The rabbinic judgment tradition pictures books opened and the wholly righteous sealed for life, the wholly wicked for death; it interprets a written mark as distinguishing moral status and fate, extending the commentary's identity-mark contrast into an eschatological register.

column5: Christ's letter written on hearts and read by all
column6: Paul calls the community a letter of Christ, written by the Spirit on human hearts and known and read by everyone; this is an inward trace that identifies its source and can be read, directly developing the commentary's mark-and-recognition relation.

column5: God's seal and Spirit in hearts
column6: Paul says God set his seal on believers and gave the Spirit in their hearts as a pledge; this specifies an inward divine mark of belonging and a lasting guarantee, distinct from the name-inscription in the commentary.

column5: circumcision interpreted as a seal of faith
column6: Paul calls Abraham's circumcision a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith he already had; this Christian reading interprets the fleshly sign in Genesis 17 as certifying an inward allegiance, adding a distinct meaning to the commentary's mark of ownership.

column5: God's servants sealed on their foreheads before harm
column6: The servants of God receive a seal on their foreheads before the earth is harmed; besides Revelation 14's names of belonging, this mark specifically distinguishes and protects a community before destruction, like Ezekiel's spared mourners.

column5: account for every careless word at judgment
column6: Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this connects the commentary's denier's spoken dismissal and God's knowledge of the open and hidden with a verbal trace that carries consequences.

column5: words justify or condemn
column6: Jesus says a person is justified or condemned by their words; this adds the words' role as evidence that distinguishes a person's standing, alongside the commentary's punishment of one who calls revelation ancient fables.

column5: hidden heart-counsels disclosed; praise from God
column6: At the Lord's coming, hidden things of darkness and heart-counsels are brought to light, and each receives praise from God; this joins concealed traces, divine recognition, and moral evaluation in a way close to the commentary's open/hidden knowledge.

column5: one tongue blesses God and curses people
column6: James says the tongue blesses the Lord and Father yet curses people made in God's likeness; it gives a specific ethical test for honoring God's name, relevant to the commentary's contrast between glorifying the Lord and contemptuous speech.

column5: gain the world and forfeit oneself
column6: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while losing or forfeiting oneself; this sharply reverses preference for worldly life and specifies its cost beside the commentary's better, lasting hereafter.

column5: sowing to flesh or Spirit yields corruption or eternal life
column6: Paul says sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; the harvested result is a trace of one's chosen orientation, directly linking preference, remainder, and lasting fate.

column5: fruit of former conduct ends in death
column6: Paul asks what fruit came from former shameful practices and says their end is death; the fruit is a readable remainder of chosen conduct, tied to the fate that contrasts with the commentary's lasting hereafter.

column5: fruit of holiness and end of eternal life
column6: Freed from sin and enslaved to God, believers bear fruit for holiness whose end is eternal life; this combines the commentary's owner relation, trace of action, and lasting destiny in one passage.

column5: acts toward the least counted as acts toward the king
column6: In the judgment scene, care for the least is counted as service to the king; deeds become the trace by which allegiance is recognized, giving a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that preference leaves an identifying mark.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The judgment ends with the two groups sent to eternal punishment or eternal life; this supplies a specific Christian formulation of the commentary's contrast between the fire-bound and the better, enduring hereafter.

column5: books opened; the dead judged by their deeds
column6: The dead are judged according to their deeds recorded in opened books; this turns the commentary's trace into an eschatological record that exposes and distinguishes each person's conduct.

column5: name absent from the book of life; lake of fire
column6: Anyone not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire; this explicitly makes a written name the mark distinguishing the saved from those assigned to fire, uniting the commentary's owner-sign and fire images.
